prerequisites: Minimum prior knowledge of General Chemistry is considered essential to follow the course and achieve its objectives. This knowledge may have been acquired in Secondary Education or may require supplementary and preliminary effort from the student before taking the course.

learning_outcomes.text: Students have demonstrated possession and understanding of knowledge in a field of study that starts from the basis of general secondary education, and is usually found at a level that, while supported by advanced textbooks, also includes some aspects that involve knowledge from the forefront of their field of study.

Students know how to apply their knowledge to their work or vocation in a professional way and possess the competencies that are usually demonstrated by the elaboration and defense of arguments and the resolution of problems within their field of study.
Students have developed those learning skills necessary to undertake further studies with a high degree of autonomy.

Basic professional knowledge. Knowledge, skills, and attitudes that enable the understanding of new theories, interpretations, methods, and techniques within different disciplinary fields, leading to optimally satisfying professional demands.

Ability to solve problems. Ability to identify, analyze, and define the significant elements that constitute a problem to solve it rigorously. The student must discern, find different strategies when determining possible solutions to the problems they face and, if there is more than one, know how to choose the most appropriate.
Teamwork. Integrate and actively collaborate in achieving common objectives with other people, areas, and organizations, in both national and international contexts.
Ability to understand and apply the principles of basic knowledge of general chemistry, organic and inorganic chemistry, and their applications in engineering.
Know and understand the ultimate origin of transformations, properties, and applications of the matter around us, expressing them in a formal chemical language.
Acquire a level of training that enables them to learn new techniques and solve new problems independently.
Acquire an essentially quantitative sense of Chemistry by performing numerical exercises that, as far as possible, refer to facts related to their future profession.
Achieve sufficient experimental training, so that they develop experimental abilities and skills.

syllabus_topics: Block 1. Structure of matter.
Block 2. Chemical reactions. Basic stoichiometric, energetic, and kinetic calculations.
Block 3. Chemical equilibria.
Block 4. Carbon chemistry.
Laboratory practice program.
Topic 1. Atomic structure and chemical bonding.
Topic 2. States of aggregation of matter.
Topic 3. Stoichiometry of chemical reactions.
Topic 4. Introduction to chemical thermodynamics.
Topic 5. Basic chemical kinetics.
Topic 6. Introduction to chemical equilibrium. Application to gaseous systems.
Topic 7. Applications of chemical equilibrium in solution: acid-base, solubility, and oxidation-reduction.
Topic 8. Introduction to carbon chemistry.
Practice 1. Separation of mixture components: distillation, filtration, and extraction. Introduction to industrial separation operations.
Practice 2. Preparation of solutions.
Practice 3. Chemical bonding and properties of substances.
Practice 4. Reaction enthalpy. Hess's Law.
Practice 5. Chemical equilibrium. Le Châtelier's Principle. Industrial application: ammonia stripping.
Practice 6. Acid-base titrations. Titration curves. Hydrolysis.
Practice 7. Oxidation-reduction equilibria. Operation of galvanic cells. Application in the production of printed circuits.

assessment_methods.method: Continuous assessment / participation in teaching group via tests (Wooclap/Kahoot)
Continuous assessment / performance in work group (lab practices) via tests (Wooclap/Kahoot)
Partial/Final exams (numerical exercises, theory, and practical questions, including formulation seminars)

assessment_rules: Attendance at laboratory practices is mandatory for first-time enrolled students and those who do not have them validated. For the ordinary call, the global grade is calculated as E1*0.1 + E2*0.05 + E3*0.05 + E4*0.1 + E5*0.7, provided that the E5 component (exams) is at least 4 out of 10. If E5 is less than 4, the global grade will be E5. E5 is the average of two partial exams if a minimum of 4 was obtained in the first partial, otherwise it is the final exam grade. The extraordinary call follows the same criteria, with E5 being the extraordinary exam grade; students without E1-E4 grades can take an equivalent test. A single final evaluation, representing 100% of the grade, consists of a broader exam that may include a practical lab evaluation and additional exercises to assess all competencies.
